props.title: Gone with the Wind
props.initialSlug: Epic Civil War romance tests Southern belle's survival

sections.content: Gone with the Wind (1939) revolutionized epic filmmaking with its sweeping portrayal of the American Civil War through the lens of the headstrong Scarlett O'Hara. Producer David O. Selznick's obsessive attention to detail and director Victor Fleming's grand vision created Hollywood's first true blockbuster, running nearly four hours. The film's Technicolor cinematography by Ernest Haller set new standards, while Max Steiner's lush orchestral score established the template for epic film music. Despite its problematic portrayal of slavery and race relations, the film's technical achievements and Vivien Leigh's fierce performance as Scarlett remain landmark accomplishments.

sections.content: The film's influence on subsequent historical epics cannot be overstated. Ben-Hur (1959) and Cleopatra (1963) followed its template of combining personal drama with historical sweep. The practical effects and massive sets of Gone with the Wind influenced everything from Doctor Zhivago (1965) to Titanic (1997). The burning of Atlanta sequence required building and burning massive sets, establishing a scale of practical effects that wouldn't be matched until the advent of CGI.

The controversial legacy of Gone with the Wind mirrors America's ongoing struggle with Civil War history. While 12 Years a Slave (2013) and Django Unchained (2012) directly confront slavery's horrors, Gone with the Wind's romanticized Old South perspective remains problematic. Yet its technical mastery and Leigh's performance as a complex, morally ambiguous female protagonist were revolutionary for 1939, influencing characters from All About Eve (1950) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). sections.content: Gone with the Wind established conventions still seen in modern epics like Gladiator (2000) and Troy (2004): the sweeping narrative scope, doomed romance amid historical upheaval, and extensive use of practical sets and effects. The film's unprecedented $3.9 million budget (over $73 million today) helped establish the blockbuster model. Even modern directors like Christopher Nolan cite its influence, with Dunkirk (2017) and Interstellar (2014) following its ambition to merge intimate human drama with epic scale.
